explanations.explanation: Paul says to "strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God." Notice the target is a place with Christ in it. It isn't a goal you'd put on a poster. I think that's a great thing to aim at, friend.

Paul never brings up reputation in this verse. He points the Colossians to "the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God." A spotless reputation is a lot of polishing on a cookie jar nobody's opening. Aim higher, baker, because that's exactly where Paul points.

That's a fair guess, but it isn't what verse 1 says. Paul says to strive for "the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God." He starts from the fact that they've been raised with Christ, so his aim is a place, not a rulebook. I think that's good news, because you can't stamp a rule into a cookie and expect it to taste like anything.

Paul writes, "For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God." Hidden with Christ, tucked in God like a batch kept safe in the oven. Nobody gets to snatch it out. That's a lot of safety packed into one sentence.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, and I get why he came to mind. But Paul says their life is "hidden with Christ in God." Moses isn't in this verse at all. Christ is the one their life is hidden with.

Abraham, a forefather of Israel, is a famous name, so no shame in reaching for him. Still, Paul says their life is "hidden with Christ in God." Abraham doesn't make an appearance in this verse. It's Christ, baker, every time.

explanations.answer: They appear with Him in glory
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory." Did you catch that? Christ IS their life, so when He appears, they appear right along with Him. Nobody gets left in the back of the line. This is one of the reasons my ovens stay ready.

explanations.answer: They are given new work to do
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention new work in this verse. He says, "When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory." Nobody hands out a clipboard here. The verse is about appearing with Him in glory.

explanations.answer: They are sent out to the nations
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like a lot of travel, but Paul doesn't say it in this verse. He says, "When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory." The picture is believers appearing with Him. So no packing a suitcase here, baker.

Yep. Paul lists "sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry." He puts greed in the same sentence as idolatry. That's a heavy list, and I think Paul meant for greed not to hide in it. Good eye, friend.
Paul really does say it. His list ends with "greed, which is idolatry." It's right there at the end of verse 5, hiding in plain sight. Greed gets named for what it is.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "When you lived among them, you also used to walk in these ways." He's talking to the Colossians about their own past, and he doesn't sugarcoat it. Paul isn't buttering them up like a fresh sheet of cookies. He's being honest, and I think that's a kindness.

Right, because Paul says "you also used to walk in these ways." The Colossians had lived among the people he just described. The key words there are "used to." That was their past, and verse 8 starts with "But now."

Paul's list says, "anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips." Anger and slander are both right there. That list is all about what comes out of us and how we treat each other. Nice catch, baker.

Pride and envy aren't on this list. Paul names "anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips." It's easy to mix them up because they all feel like they belong together. Just read the verse closely, friend, and the list is right there.

Those two don't show up in verse 8. Paul's list is "anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips." No laziness, no grumbling. I think a lot of us could put our own names on a different list, but this one is Paul's.

Paul says they "have put on the new self." Off with the old, on with the new. And he adds that this new self "is being renewed," so it's still being worked on. I can relate, because I got renewed once and I'm still getting the hang of it.
That's a smart guess, since people talk about the inner self all the time. But Paul's word is "new." He says they "have put on the new self." It's about a whole change of clothes, baker.

Free is a lovely word, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says they "have put on the new self." The word is new, and it comes right after taking off the old self. Stick with Paul's own word, friend.
Paul says the new self "is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator." So the pattern isn't a person down here. It's the One who made it. That's the best blueprint a baker could ask for.

Teachers do a lot of good, but Paul doesn't name them here. He says the new self is renewed "in the image of its Creator." The model is the Creator Himself, not the people who point us to Him. I think that's a relief, because teachers are only human.

Ancestors aren't in this verse. Paul says the new self is being renewed "in knowledge in the image of its Creator." So the pattern isn't something handed down through a family recipe card. It comes from the Creator.

It's the other way around. Paul says, "Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free." Those dividing lines don't hold here. Instead, "Christ is all and is in all."

Right. Paul says, "Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all." He runs through the whole list and none of those lines stands. And the verse ends on Christ being all and in all, which is the best part.

Paul says to clothe yourselves "with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience." Compassion and kindness are right at the front of that outfit. That's quite a wardrobe, friend. And the best part is, it's meant for the elect of God, holy and beloved.

Courage and strength are good words, but they aren't in Paul's list. He says, "hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience." This outfit is soft and warm, not a suit of armor. I think that's worth noticing.

Those two sound nice, but they aren't in this verse. Paul lists "hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience." Humility is on there, which is kind of the opposite of showing off. Take another look at the verse, baker, and the list is all there.

Paul doesn't put that condition on it. He says, "Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else." There's no "after they make it right" anywhere in the verse. He gives the pattern right after: "Forgive as the Lord forgave you."

That's what Paul says. He tells them to "forgive any complaint you may have against someone else," and he doesn't add a condition. Then he gives the measure: "Forgive as the Lord forgave you." Any complaint, baker, so no leftovers.

Paul says, "And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity." Love goes on over everything else, like the last layer before you head out the door. And it's the bond that holds it all together. Even a mustache needs wax, friend, and this outfit needs love.

Faith is a good one, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says to put on "love, which is the bond of perfect unity." Love is the piece that goes over all the rest. I think that's worth remembering.

Joy is a fine thing to wear, believe me, but Paul's word here is love. He says, "And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity." Love is the one called the bond of perfect unity. Joy didn't get that title in this verse.

explanations.answer: They were called to it as one body
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body." The reason is their calling, and they were called together. One body means nobody is baking alone, friend. And then comes that short line: "And be thankful."

explanations.answer: It keeps their enemies far away
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about enemies here. His reason is, "for to this you were called as members of one body." The peace of Christ is tied to their calling together. It's about the body, baker.

explanations.answer: It earns them the favor of God
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that as the reason. He says, "for to this you were called as members of one body." The reason is that they were called to peace as one body. Nothing in the verse talks about earning anything, friend.

Paul says, "Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom." The word dwells in them, and it spills out as they teach and admonish each other. Admonish just means to gently warn and guide. Good one, baker.

It's actually true. Paul writes, "Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom." Teaching and admonishing one another is part of what he describes. And he adds that it's done "with all wisdom."

explanations.answer: Do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus." Word or deed, everything goes under His name. It's a very big net. I'm glad it covers a batch of burnt cookies too.

explanations.answer: Do it all by the rules of the elders
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that here. He says, "whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus." The name that matters in this verse is the Lord Jesus. Not a set of rules, friend.

explanations.answer: Do it all where the church can see
explanations.explanation: That isn't in this verse. Paul says, "whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus." It's about whose name it's done in, not who's watching. I think that frees us up a lot, baker.

That's right. Paul ends the verse with, "giving thanks to God the Father through Him." The thanks goes to God the Father, and it goes through the Lord Jesus. Thankfulness shows up again and again in this passage, baker.

It's true, though. Paul says to do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, "giving thanks to God the Father through Him." Thanks goes to the Father, through Jesus. This is the third time Paul talks about being thankful in this stretch, so he clearly means it.
